meta.title: Who really said "Life is suffering"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not a sentence the Buddha ever spoke — it is a three-word compression of the First Noble Truth. The Pali of SN 56.11 gives a list of things that are dukkha, and 'suffering' is widely argued to be a poor rendering of dukkha.
meta.ogDescription: A translation problem, not a fake. The Pali says 'this is the noble truth of dukkha' and then lists — birth, ageing, illness, death. It never says life is suffering.

answer.label: The teaching is the Buddha's — the three-word English is not
answer.authorDates: fl. c. 5th century BCE · founder of Buddhism — the teaching is his; the wording is a modern compression
answer.sourceLine: This is a translation dispute, not a fabrication. Behind it stands a real and central passage: the First Noble Truth as set out in the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta (Saṃyutta Nikāya 56.11). But the Pali does not contain a sentence equivalent to ‘life is suffering.’ It reads Idaṃ kho pana, bhikkhave, dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ — ‘now this, monks, is the noble truth of dukkha’ — and then lists: birth, ageing, illness, death, union with what you dislike, separation from what you love, not getting what you want. Two things are lost in the squeeze: dukkha is not simply ‘suffering,’ and a list of conditions is not a verdict on existence.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: Idaṁ kho pana, bhikkhave, dukkhaṁ ariyasaccaṁ—jātipi dukkhā, jarāpi dukkhā, byādhipi dukkho, maraṇampi dukkhaṁ, appiyehi sampayogo dukkho, piyehi vippayogo dukkho, yampicchaṁ na labhati tampi dukkhaṁ—saṅkhittena pañcupādānakkhandhā dukkhā.
trail: We went to the Pali. SuttaCentral’s Mahāsaṅgīti edition of SN 56.11 gives the First Noble Truth as a naming plus an enumeration: this is the noble truth of dukkha, then birth, ageing, illness, death, and three kinds of thwarted wanting, closing with saṅkhittena pañcupādānakkhandhā dukkhā — ‘in brief, the five clinging-aggregates are dukkha.’ Grammatically there is no proposition ‘life is X’ anywhere in it the Pali text ↗.

Then we checked whether ‘suffering’ is even the standard rendering. It is not universal: Thanissaro Bhikkhu translates the whole passage with stress — ‘Now this, monks, is the noble truth of stress: Birth is stressful, aging is stressful, death is stressful…’ Access to Insight ↗.

And the objection is not a modern internet quibble. Walpola Rahula, in What the Buddha Taught, writes that translating the First Noble Truth as ‘The Noble Truth of Suffering’ and reading it to mean ‘life according to Buddhism is nothing but suffering and pain’ is ‘highly unsatisfactory and misleading’ — and concludes it is better to leave dukkha untranslated than to render it ‘suffering.’

Even the first great English translator did not use the word. Max Müller, rendering sabbe saṅkhārā dukkhā at Dhammapada 278 in 1881, wrote ‘All created things are grief and pain’ Müller’s Dhammapada ↗.
source.excerptNote: The Pali of the First Noble Truth. Read the shape of it rather than the vocabulary: a heading and then a list of seven specific human situations, ending with a technical summary. It is closer to a diagnosis than to a slogan — and every item on the list is an occasion, not a totality.

source.rightsNote: Mixed, so pick your text carefully. The Pali is ancient and free. Among English versions, Max Müller’s 1881 Dhammapada (Sacred Books of the East X) is public domain and safe to quote, as is T. W. Rhys Davids’ 1881 rendering of this sutta in the same series. Modern translations are not: Thanissaro Bhikkhu’s ‘stress’ version is released for free distribution under its own terms rather than into the public domain, and Bhikkhu Bodhi’s Wisdom Publications translations are fully in copyright. We give no blanket rights tag here because the answer differs per translator. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Gautama Buddha
author.heading: The Buddha and the word dukkha
author.metaLine: fl. c. 5th century BCE · founder of Buddhism · northern India
author.bio: Siddhārtha Gautama taught in Magadha and Kosala in roughly the fifth century BCE, and the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta is presented as his first discourse after awakening. He taught in an Indic vernacular; the record we have is in Pali, preserved orally for centuries before it was written down. That matters here more than usual. The whole of this dispute turns on one Pali noun, dukkha, which he used as a technical term across thousands of passages — and which no single English word has ever managed to carry.

cite.sourceCitation: Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, Saṃyutta Nikāya 56.11, Pali Canon. Pali text: Mahāsaṅgīti edition (SuttaCentral). ‘Life is suffering’ is a modern English compression, not a translation of any sentence in it.
cite.pageCitation: Quotle.info. “Who really said ‘Life is suffering’?” Last verified 21 Jul 2026.

copyAttribution: A three-word English compression of the First Noble Truth (Saṃyutta Nikāya 56.11). The Pali names the truth of dukkha and then lists; it never says life is suffering.

misattribution.heading: What the compression loses
misattribution.intro: Nobody invented this one to sell a poster. It is a real teaching squeezed through a bad English word and then squeezed again into three syllables — and each squeeze costs something specific.

items.why: Translators reach for unsatisfactoriness, stress, unease, dis-ease, incompleteness. Thanissaro Bhikkhu uses ‘stress’ throughout; Max Müller wrote ‘grief and pain’; Walpola Rahula argued it is better left untranslated. ‘Suffering’ catches the acute end and drops the everyday end — the low hum of things not quite fitting a 'stress' translation ↗.

The Pali says ‘this is the noble truth of dukkha’ and enumerates: birth, ageing, illness, death, being stuck with what you dislike, losing what you love, not getting what you want. Turning that into ‘life is suffering’ converts a set of occasions into a claim about the whole of existence — which is precisely the pessimism Rahula said the bad translation had produced.

The First Noble Truth is the first of four, and the remaining three are about cause, cessation and a path. Quoting the first alone is like quoting a diagnosis and skipping the prognosis and the treatment. As a standalone epigram it reverses the point of the sequence.

You will often read that dukkha comes from du- (bad) plus kha (axle-hole) — a wheel that wobbles on its axle. It is a lovely image and it is genuinely repeated by respected teachers, but philologists more commonly derive it from Sanskrit duḥ-sthā, ‘standing badly, unsteady.’ Use the wheel as an illustration, not as a fact about the word’s history the two derivations ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: A real teaching in a poor English coat. The Pali of SN 56.11 names the noble truth of dukkha and lists seven occasions of it; ‘life is suffering’ is a modern compression that no translator produced the Pali ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: Three words, and they sound like the bottom line of a whole religion. That is the appeal and the trouble: it is short enough to be a tattoo and blunt enough to end a conversation, so it has become the one thing everybody thinks they know about Buddhism.

The irony is that a tradition built on precision about mental states gets summarised in the least precise word available. Ask someone who has read the Pali and they will usually say the same thing: it is not that life is agony, it is that nothing quite holds still enough to satisfy you — which is a much stranger and more interesting claim.
detailsBody: Birth, ageing, illness and death — the four unavoidable physical passages.
Union with what is disliked, and separation from what is loved — the two social ones.
Not getting what one wants — the ordinary, daily one.
‘In brief, the five clinging-aggregates are dukkha’ — the technical summary that reframes the whole list as being about clinging rather than about circumstance.
Note what is not on the list: living, breathing, eating, working, loving. The Pali never puts ‘life’ in the subject position.
context.pull: The Pali names a truth and then lists seven situations. Not one of them is 'life'.
